segments.say: It's Monday evening, and Ben has had a long day at work. He looks at the laptop on the kitchen table, and a very reasonable thought arrives. I'm not really in the mood tonight. I'll feel more like it tomorrow. And it sounds so sensible. After all, surely a speech written in the right mood will be better than one squeezed out of a tired evening.

That's the fifth popular belief we'll look at tonight. The idea that we should wait until we feel like doing something. That motivation comes first, and action follows. Timothy Pychyl, whom we met earlier, has written about this thought many times. He describes it as one of the most common things procrastinators tell themselves, and one of the most misleading.

show.sub: I'll feel more like it tomorrow

segments.say: Here's the trouble. Tomorrow, the task will bring up exactly the same feelings it brings up today. The same unease, the same uncertainty, the same small knot. Those feelings aren't attached to the day. They're attached to the task. So waiting for a better mood often means waiting for something that never quite arrives. And meanwhile, the deadline keeps creeping closer.

show.text: I'll feel more like doing it tomorrow.
show.by: One of the most common things we tell ourselves

segments.say: Many people discover something surprising when they try it the other way round. If they begin anyway, even in a grey mood, the mood often changes after a few minutes. The task turns out to be a little more interesting than it looked from the outside. Interest and confidence grow as we work, not before. In other words, feeling like it is often a result of starting, not a ticket we need in order to start.

So there are two ways to approach a task. We can wait until we feel like it, and then start. Or we can start a little, and then see how it feels. The first way sounds kinder, but it often leaves us waiting. The second way asks for just a few minutes of courage, and then lets our feelings catch up.

show.title: Two ways to begin
items: Wait to feel like it, then start
Start a little, then see how it feels

segments.say: So why do some people seem to hesitate more than others? A team of researchers at Ruhr University Bochum in Germany explored this with brain scans, in a study published in 2018. They asked a few hundred adults about how easily they turn their intentions into action, and how often they hesitate and put things off. Then they looked at the structure and activity of their brains.

They found two things that stood out. People who tended to hesitate more had, on average, a somewhat larger amygdala, a small almond-shaped region deep in the brain that's involved in emotions, especially in sensing possible threats. And the connection between the amygdala and an area near the front of the brain, which helps decide which actions to take, seemed to be weaker.

show.what: Brain scans of people who act quickly and people who tend to hesitate

segments.say: One way the researchers interpreted it was this. People who hesitate more may be a little more sensitive to the possible downsides of an action, and a little less able to quiet that worry and move ahead. It fits beautifully with the idea that procrastination is about feelings. But it's one study, the links were averages, and brain shape is never a sentence. Brains change with practice and experience.

show.cap: Feeling and doing, side by side

segments.say: For Ben, it might mean his brain is simply quick to notice everything that could go wrong in a speech. The jokes that might fall flat. The tears that might come. That's not a flaw. It's part of caring. But it does mean that the first step needs to feel safe and small, so the alarm has nothing very big to ring about.

So Ben makes a small decision. Next time, he won't wait to feel like it. He'll sit down for ten minutes and see what happens. If it's awful, he can stop. The knot will probably still be there when he opens the laptop. But he's beginning to suspect that the knot isn't a stop sign. It's just a feeling, and feelings can come along for the ride.

It's worth noticing how often this happens in everyday life. The cold swim that feels impossible from the edge of the pool, and lovely after a minute in the water. The tidy-up that feels endless until you pick up the first cup. The walk you didn't want to take that turns into the best part of the day. In each case, the reluctance arrives first, and the good feeling arrives later.
